question.stem: When working in the MongoDB shell, what does the statement `use campusDB` accomplish before any write command is issued?

options.A: It selects `campusDB` as the active session context in memory without creating disk files yet
options.B: It immediately writes a 1 GB empty database file to the server disk
options.C: It drops the previous database from the storage engine
options.D: It lists all collections inside `campusDB` on the terminal

answer.explanation: `use <databaseName>` switches the current database context for subsequent commands, but MongoDB does not create the database on disk until data is inserted into a collection within it. (Key Takeaway: `use` switches the active database context lazily in memory.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 1. Database Operations & Storage Lifecycle > Database Context Switching & Creation ("use <databaseName>")

question.stem: Which shell command outputs the list of all databases on the connected server together with their gigabyte sizes (`0.000GB`)?

options.A: `show collections`
options.B: `db.getDatabases()`
options.C: `show dbs`
options.D: `use dbs`

answer.explanation: `show dbs` lists every populated database on the connected MongoDB server along with its storage size (such as `admin 0.000GB` and `schoolDB 0.000GB`). (Key Takeaway: `show dbs` reports all populated databases and their disk sizes.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 1. Database Operations & Storage Lifecycle > Database Catalog Inspection ("show dbs")

question.stem: What is the irreversible result of invoking `db.dropDatabase()` while `schoolDB` is the active database context?

options.A: Only empty collections inside `schoolDB` are removed
options.B: `schoolDB` along with all of its collections and documents is permanently deleted
options.C: Only the first collection in `schoolDB` is dropped
options.D: `schoolDB` is renamed to `local` in `show dbs`

answer.explanation: `db.dropDatabase()` permanently deletes the currently selected database (`schoolDB`), including all of its collections and documents, and cannot be undone. (Key Takeaway: `db.dropDatabase()` permanently removes the active database and all its contents.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 1. Database Operations & Storage Lifecycle > Database Destruction & Removal ("db.dropDatabase()")

question.stem: In `db.createCollection(<name>, <options>)`, what is the purpose of the optional second `<options>` parameter?

options.A: To pass an initial array of student documents for bulk insertion
options.B: To specify sort order and pagination limits for `find()` queries
options.C: To configure collection-level settings such as schema validation rules or a capped collection size
options.D: To specify which fields should be excluded from projections

answer.explanation: While MongoDB auto-creates collections on first insert, explicit creation with `db.createCollection(name, options)` lets you set collection options such as validation rules or a capped size. (Key Takeaway: The `<options>` parameter in `db.createCollection()` configures validation rules or capped storage.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 2. Collection Architecture & Structural Management > Collection Creation Mechanics ("db.createCollection()")

question.stem: How does a developer list all collections currently stored inside the active `schoolDB` database?

options.A: Run `show collections` after selecting `schoolDB` with `use schoolDB`
options.B: Run `show dbs` with `{ schoolDB: 1 }`
options.C: Run `db.createCollection("list")`
options.D: Run `db.schoolDB.findOne()`

answer.explanation: After switching to `schoolDB` via `use schoolDB`, running `show collections` lists every collection that has been created explicitly or implicitly in that database. (Key Takeaway: `show collections` enumerates all collections in the active database.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 2. Collection Architecture & Structural Management > Collection Inventory Inspection ("show collections")

question.stem: What happens to the indexes of the `students` collection when `db.students.drop()` is executed?

options.A: All indexes on `students` are preserved in the database for future collections
options.B: Only the `_id` index is deleted while secondary indexes remain active
options.C: The `students` collection, all of its documents, and all of its indexes are permanently removed
options.D: The command fails unless all indexes are manually dropped first

answer.explanation: `db.<collection>.drop()` permanently removes a collection, all of the documents it contains, and any indexes defined on it. (Key Takeaway: `db.<collection>.drop()` deletes the collection, its documents, and its indexes.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 2. Collection Architecture & Structural Management > Collection Removal & Destruction ("db.<collection>.drop()")

question.stem: Which command inserts two student documents (`Meera` aged `17` and `Kabir` aged `18`) into `db.students` in a single call?

options.A: `db.students.insertOne([{ name: "Meera", age: 17 }, { name: "Kabir", age: 18 }])`
options.B: `db.students.insertMany([{ name: "Meera", age: 17 }, { name: "Kabir", age: 18 }])`
options.C: `db.students.insertMany({ name: "Meera", age: 17 }, { name: "Kabir", age: 18 })`
options.D: `db.students.updateMany({}, [{ name: "Meera", age: 17 }, { name: "Kabir", age: 18 }])`

answer.explanation: `insertMany([doc1, doc2, ...])` inserts multiple documents into a collection in a single call when passed as a JavaScript array `[...]`. (Key Takeaway: Use `insertMany([...])` with an array of document objects for batch insertion.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 3. Document Ingestion Mechanics (CRUD Create) > Batch Document Ingestion ("insertMany()")

question.stem: How does `db.students.find({ age: 18 })` differ from `db.students.findOne({ age: 18 })` in what it returns to the caller?

options.A: `find()` returns a cursor over all matching documents, whereas `findOne()` returns the first matching document object (or `null`)
options.B: `find()` returns `null` when multiple matches exist, whereas `findOne()` returns an array
options.C: `find()` modifies matching documents, whereas `findOne()` is read-only
options.D: `find()` only inspects the first document in the collection, whereas `findOne()` scans all documents

answer.explanation: `find(query, projection)` retrieves all matching documents and returns a cursor, whereas `findOne(query, projection)` retrieves only the first matching document (or `null`) instead of a cursor. (Key Takeaway: `find()` returns a multi-document cursor; `findOne()` returns one document or `null`.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 4. Document Retrieval & Query Architecture (CRUD Read) > Cursor-Based Querying ("find()")

question.stem: Which query returns only the `name` field (and suppresses `_id`) for the first student whose `grade` is `8` or higher?

options.A: `db.students.find({ grade: { $gte: 8 } }, { name: 1, _id: 0 })`
options.B: `db.students.findOne({ grade: { $gte: 8 } }, { name: 1, _id: 0 })`
options.C: `db.students.findOne({ grade: { $gt: 8 } }, { name: 1, _id: 1 })`
options.D: `db.students.findOne({ grade: { $lte: 8 } }, { name: 0, _id: 0 })`

answer.explanation: `findOne()` returns only the first matching document, `{ grade: { $gte: 8 } }` filters for grade 8 or higher, and `{ name: 1, _id: 0 }` includes `name` while excluding `_id`. (Key Takeaway: `findOne({ grade: { $gte: 8 } }, { name: 1, _id: 0 })` projects a single field from the first match.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 4. Document Retrieval & Query Architecture (CRUD Read) > Single Document Lookup ("findOne()")

question.stem: In `db.students.find({}, { name: 1, age: 1, _id: 0 })`, what role does the first empty object `{}` play?

options.A: It suppresses all fields except `_id`
options.B: It acts as an empty query filter that matches every document in the `students` collection
options.C: It sorts the output in ascending order of insertion
options.D: It deletes unmatched fields from disk

answer.explanation: In `find(query, projection)`, the first argument is the query filter; passing an empty filter `{}` matches every document in the collection so the second argument `{ name: 1, age: 1, _id: 0 }` can project fields across all records. (Key Takeaway: An empty query filter `{}` in `find({}, projection)` matches all documents.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 5. Advanced Query Filtering, Projection & Pagination > Field Projection Mechanics

question.stem: What order is produced by executing `db.students.find().sort({ grade: -1 })`?

options.A: Students are ordered from lowest to highest `grade` (ascending)
options.B: Students are ordered from highest to lowest `grade` (descending)
options.C: All students with negative `grade` values are deleted
options.D: Only the last student in the collection is returned

answer.explanation: `sort({ field: 1 | -1 })` orders query results where `1` denotes ascending order and `-1` denotes descending order; thus `sort({ grade: -1 })` orders students from highest to lowest grade. (Key Takeaway: `sort({ field: -1 })` sorts results in descending order.)

question.stem: Which operator tests whether a field value is not equal to a specified value inside a MongoDB query filter?

options.A: `$nin`
options.B: `$lt`
options.C: `$ne`
options.D: `$pull`

answer.explanation: In the comparison operators table, `$ne` represents 'Not equal' for testing inequality against a value, whereas `$nin` tests whether a value is not in an array and `$pull` removes elements from an array during updates. (Key Takeaway: `$ne` is the scalar not-equal comparison operator.)

question.stem: If a developer wants to update Rahul's `grade` to `10` without altering his `name` or `subjects` fields, which command should be executed?

options.A: `db.students.updateOne({ name: "Rahul" }, { $set: { grade: 10 } })`
options.B: `db.students.updateOne({ name: "Rahul" }, { $inc: { grade: 10 } })`
options.C: `db.students.updateOne({ name: "Rahul" }, { $push: { grade: 10 } })`
options.D: `db.students.insertOne({ name: "Rahul", grade: 10 })`

answer.explanation: `db.students.updateOne({ name: "Rahul" }, { $set: { grade: 10 } })` updates the first document matching `{ name: "Rahul" }` and uses `$set` to set `grade` to `10` without replacing the whole document. (Key Takeaway: `updateOne()` with `$set` updates specific fields in place.)

question.stem: A school administrator runs `db.students.deleteMany({ age: 17 })` on a collection containing 12 students aged 17 and 30 students aged 18; what remains in `students`?

options.A: 11 students aged 17 and 30 students aged 18
options.B: 0 students aged 17 and 30 students aged 18
options.C: 0 documents because `deleteMany()` always empties the entire collection
options.D: The `students` collection is dropped from `schoolDB`

answer.explanation: `deleteMany({ age: 17 })` deletes every document matching the filter `{ age: 17 }` (all 12 of them) while leaving the 30 documents with `{ age: 18 }` untouched in the collection. (Key Takeaway: `deleteMany(filter)` removes all documents matching the filter and preserves non-matching documents.)

question.stem: Which query combines logical disjunction and comparison filtering to find students who either have `age` greater than or equal to `19` OR have `name` equal to `"Rahul"`?

options.A: `db.students.find({ $and: [{ age: { $gte: 19 } }, { name: "Rahul" }] })`
options.B: `db.students.find({ $or: [{ age: { $gte: 19 } }, { name: "Rahul" }] })`
options.C: `db.students.find({ $in: [{ age: 19 }, { name: "Rahul" }] })`
options.D: `db.students.find({ age: { $gt: 19 }, name: "Rahul" })`

answer.explanation: The `$or` logical operator takes an array of condition objects (`[{ age: { $gte: 19 } }, { name: "Rahul" }]`) and matches any document satisfying at least one condition. (Key Takeaway: Use `$or: [cond1, cond2]` to express logical OR across multiple field predicates.)

question.stem: Which operational rules govern database creation and visibility in MongoDB (`use <databaseName>` and `show dbs`) (Select all that apply)?

options.A: MongoDB does not provide a dedicated command to create an empty database ahead of time
options.B: Executing `use schoolDB` immediately creates `schoolDB` on disk before any collection write
options.C: `show dbs` lists all databases selected with `use`, even if they contain zero collections
options.D: A database only appears in `show dbs` once data has actually been inserted into a collection within it
options.E: `use schoolDB` only applies to the single next command and then resets to `admin`

answer.explanation: MongoDB has no dedicated command to pre-create a database (A); `use <databaseName>` selects the context for all subsequent commands in the session, and the database is created on disk and listed in `show dbs` only once data is written to it (D). (Key Takeaway: Databases are lazily materialized on first collection write.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 1. Database Operations & Storage Lifecycle > Database Context Switching & Creation ("use <databaseName>") > Lazy Allocation Mechanics

question.stem: Which statements accurately describe explicit and implicit collection lifecycle operations in MongoDB (Select all that apply)?

options.A: Inserting into a non-existent collection with `insertOne()` fails unless `db.createCollection()` was called first
options.B: `db.createCollection(name, options)` explicitly creates a collection and supports setting validation rules or capped size
options.C: `show collections` lists every collection that exists in the currently selected database
options.D: `db.students.drop()` removes documents from `students` but leaves its indexes intact
options.E: A collection appears in `show collections` once created either explicitly via `db.createCollection()` or implicitly via a first insert

answer.explanation: `db.createCollection(name, options)` explicitly creates a collection for options like validation rules or capped size (B); `show collections` lists all collections in the active database (C); and collections appear in `show collections` once created explicitly or implicitly via first insert (E). (Key Takeaway: Collections can be created explicitly or implicitly and are listed via `show collections`.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 2. Collection Architecture & Structural Management

question.stem: When comparing `db.students.insertOne()` and `db.students.insertMany()` for document ingestion, which statements are valid (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `insertOne()` accepts an array of multiple documents `[doc1, doc2]` to insert them individually
options.B: `insertOne(document)` inserts a single document object into the target collection
options.C: `insertMany()` requires the target collection to be pre-created with `db.createCollection()`
options.D: `insertMany()` accepts multiple documents as comma-separated arguments without square brackets
options.E: `insertMany([doc1, doc2, ...])` inserts multiple documents in a single call when passed as an array

answer.explanation: `insertOne(document)` inserts a single document (B), and `insertMany([doc1, doc2, ...])` inserts multiple documents in a single call passed as an array (E). Both auto-create the collection if it does not exist yet. (Key Takeaway: Use `insertOne(doc)` for one document and `insertMany([doc1, doc2])` for an array of documents.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 3. Document Ingestion Mechanics (CRUD Create)

question.stem: Which characteristics distinguish `db.students.find()` from `db.students.findOne()` during read operations (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `find(query, projection)` returns a cursor over all matching documents
options.B: `findOne(query, projection)` supports chaining `.sort()`, `.skip()`, and `.limit()` directly
options.C: `findOne(query, projection)` returns the first matching document object or `null` if none match
options.D: Both `find()` and `findOne()` accept a query filter as their first argument and a projection as their second argument
options.E: `find()` with no arguments returns `null`

answer.explanation: `find()` returns a cursor over all matching documents (A), `findOne()` returns a single document or `null` without supporting cursor methods like `.sort()` or `.limit()` (C), and both accept `(query, projection)` arguments (D). (Key Takeaway: Both `find()` and `findOne()` accept `(query, projection)`, returning a cursor vs. a single document/null.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 4. Document Retrieval & Query Architecture (CRUD Read)

question.stem: In `db.students.find({}, { name: 1, grade: 1, _id: 0 })`, which projection rules are demonstrated (Select all that apply)?

options.A: Setting a field to `1` excludes that field from the returned documents
options.B: Setting `_id: 0` deletes the `_id` primary key from the collection on disk
options.C: Setting `name: 1` and `grade: 1` includes those fields in the returned documents
options.D: Omitting `_id: 0` would still exclude `_id` automatically whenever `name: 1` is specified
options.E: Setting `_id: 0` explicitly excludes the `_id` field from the returned documents

answer.explanation: In a projection object, `1` includes a field (`name: 1, grade: 1`, C) and `0` excludes a field (`_id: 0`, E). Without `_id: 0`, MongoDB includes `_id` by default even when other fields are set to `1`. (Key Takeaway: Projections use `1` to include fields and `_id: 0` to suppress the default `_id` field.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 5. Advanced Query Filtering, Projection & Pagination > Field Projection Mechanics

question.stem: How does the chained query `db.students.find().sort({ grade: 1 }).skip(10).limit(5)` process documents in `students` (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `sort({ grade: 1 })` orders the matched documents in ascending order of `grade`
options.B: `skip(10)` omits the first 10 documents from the sorted result set
options.C: `sort({ grade: 1 })` restricts output to students in grade 1 only
options.D: `limit(5)` caps the number of returned documents to at most 5 after skipping 10
options.E: `limit(5)` permanently deletes all documents beyond the 5th record

answer.explanation: `sort({ grade: 1 })` sorts results in ascending order of `grade` (A), `skip(10)` skips the first 10 results (B), and `limit(5)` returns at most the next 5 documents (D). (Key Takeaway: Combining `sort()`, `skip()`, and `limit()` implements deterministic result pagination.)

question.stem: Which filter expressions accurately match their stated query semantics in MongoDB (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `{ age: { $gt: 18 } }` matches students whose `age` is `18` or higher
options.B: `{ age: { $in: [17, 18, 19] } }` matches students whose `age` equals `17`, `18`, or `19`
options.C: `{ age: { $lte: 18 } }` matches students whose `age` is less than or equal to `18`
options.D: `{ age: { $nin: [17, 18] } }` matches only students whose `age` is `17` or `18`
options.E: `{ $and: [{ age: { $gte: 18 } }, { promoted: true }] }` matches students who satisfy both conditions simultaneously

answer.explanation: `$in: [17, 18, 19]` matches any value in the array (B), `$lte: 18` matches values less than or equal to 18 (C), and `$and: [...]` matches documents satisfying all sub-conditions (E). Option A requires `$gte: 18`, and Option D describes `$in` rather than `$nin`. (Key Takeaway: Verify inclusive vs. strict bounds (`$gte` vs. `$gt`) and array inclusion vs. exclusion (`$in` vs. `$nin`).)

question.stem: When mutating documents with `db.students.updateOne()` and `db.students.updateMany()`, which execution rules apply (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `updateOne(filter, update)` updates only the first document that matches the query filter
options.B: `updateOne(filter, update)` replaces the entire document and deletes any field not listed in `$set`
options.C: `updateMany(filter, update)` applies the update operators to every document matching the query filter
options.D: `updateMany(filter, update)` can only modify a maximum of two documents per call
options.E: Neither `updateOne()` nor `updateMany()` supports the `$set` operator

answer.explanation: `updateOne(filter, update)` modifies the first matching document using operators like `$set` without replacing the whole document (A), while `updateMany(filter, update)` applies the same update to every matching document in the collection (C). (Key Takeaway: `updateOne()` updates the first match in place; `updateMany()` updates all matches in place.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 6. Field Modification & In-Place Update Operators (CRUD Update) > Update Scope & Execution Methods

question.stem: Examine the update operators `$set`, `$inc`, `$push`, and `$pull`; which descriptions accurately match their behavior on a student document (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `{ $set: { age: 20 } }` sets or replaces the `age` field value with `20`
options.B: `{ $inc: { attempts: 1 } }` overwrites `attempts` with `1` regardless of its previous numeric value
options.C: `{ $push: { subjects: "History" } }` removes `"History"` from the `subjects` array
options.D: `{ $inc: { attempts: 1 } }` adds `1` to the existing numeric value of `attempts`
options.E: `{ $pull: { subjects: "Science" } }` removes `"Science"` from the `subjects` array

answer.explanation: `$set` replaces a field's value (A), `$inc` adds to a numeric field (D), `$push` adds an element to an array, and `$pull` removes matching elements from an array (E). (Key Takeaway: `$set` assigns values, `$inc` increments numbers, `$push` appends to arrays, and `$pull` removes from arrays.)

mindmap.path: VVIT MongoDB: Databases, Collections & CRUD Operations > 6. Field Modification & In-Place Update Operators (CRUD Update) > Atomic Field Update Operators

question.stem: An engineer is deciding between `db.students.deleteOne({ age: 17 })`, `db.students.deleteMany({ age: 17 })`, and `db.students.deleteMany({})`; which statements are true (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `db.students.deleteOne({ age: 17 })` deletes all documents where `age` equals `17`
options.B: `db.students.deleteMany({ age: 17 })` deletes every document in `students` where `age` equals `17`
options.C: `db.students.deleteMany({})` drops the `students` collection and all of its indexes from `schoolDB`
options.D: `db.students.deleteMany({})` deletes all documents in `students` without dropping the collection itself
options.E: `db.students.deleteOne({ age: 17 })` deletes the `age` field from the document while keeping the document in `students`

answer.explanation: `deleteMany({ age: 17 })` removes every document where `age` equals `17` (B), and `deleteMany({})` with an empty filter deletes all documents in the collection without dropping the collection itself (D). `deleteOne({ age: 17 })` deletes the entire first matching document. (Key Takeaway: `deleteMany(filter)` removes all matching documents, and `deleteMany({})` empties the collection without dropping it.)

question.stem: Which operational rules govern database creation and visibility in MongoDB (`use <databaseName>` and `show dbs`) (Select all that apply)?

options.A: MongoDB does not provide a dedicated command to create an empty database ahead of time
options.B: Executing `use schoolDB` immediately creates `schoolDB` on disk before any collection write
options.C: `show dbs` lists all databases selected with `use`, even if they contain zero collections
options.D: A database only appears in `show dbs` once data has actually been inserted into a collection within it
options.E: `use schoolDB` only applies to the single next command and then resets to `admin`

answer.explanation: MongoDB has no dedicated command to pre-create a database (A); `use <databaseName>` selects the context for all subsequent commands in the session, and the database is created on disk and listed in `show dbs` only once data is written to it (D). (Key Takeaway: Databases are lazily materialized on first collection write.)

question.stem: In `db.students.find({}, { name: 1, grade: 1, _id: 0 })`, which projection rules are demonstrated (Select all that apply)?

options.A: Setting a field to `1` excludes that field from the returned documents
options.B: Setting `_id: 0` deletes the `_id` primary key from the collection on disk
options.C: Setting `name: 1` and `grade: 1` includes those fields in the returned documents
options.D: Omitting `_id: 0` would still exclude `_id` automatically whenever `name: 1` is specified

question.stem: Which filter expressions accurately match their stated query semantics in MongoDB (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `{ age: { $gt: 18 } }` matches students whose `age` is `18` or higher
options.B: `{ age: { $in: [17, 18, 19] } }` matches students whose `age` equals `17`, `18`, or `19`
options.C: `{ age: { $lte: 18 } }` matches students whose `age` is less than or equal to `18`
options.D: `{ age: { $nin: [17, 18] } }` matches only students whose `age` is `17` or `18`
options.E: `{ $and: [{ age: { $gte: 18 } }, { promoted: true }] }` matches students who satisfy both conditions simultaneously

answer.explanation: `$in: [17, 18, 19]` matches any value in the array (B), `$lte: 18` matches values less than or equal to 18 (C), and `$and: [...]` matches documents satisfying all sub-conditions (E). Option A requires `$gte: 18`, and Option D describes `$in` rather than `$nin`. (Key Takeaway: Verify inclusive vs. strict bounds (`$gte` vs. `$gt`) and array inclusion vs. exclusion (`$in` vs. `$nin`).)

question.stem: When mutating documents with `db.students.updateOne()` and `db.students.updateMany()`, which execution rules apply (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `updateOne(filter, update)` updates only the first document that matches the query filter
options.B: `updateOne(filter, update)` replaces the entire document and deletes any field not listed in `$set`
options.C: `updateMany(filter, update)` applies the update operators to every document matching the query filter
options.D: `updateMany(filter, update)` can only modify a maximum of two documents per call
options.E: Neither `updateOne()` nor `updateMany()` supports the `$set` operator

answer.explanation: `updateOne(filter, update)` modifies the first matching document using operators like `$set` without replacing the whole document (A), while `updateMany(filter, update)` applies the same update to every matching document in the collection (C). (Key Takeaway: `updateOne()` updates the first match in place; `updateMany()` updates all matches in place.)

question.stem: Examine the update operators `$set`, `$inc`, `$push`, and `$pull`; which descriptions accurately match their behavior on a student document (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `{ $set: { age: 20 } }` sets or replaces the `age` field value with `20`
options.B: `{ $inc: { attempts: 1 } }` overwrites `attempts` with `1` regardless of its previous numeric value
options.C: `{ $push: { subjects: "History" } }` removes `"History"` from the `subjects` array
options.D: `{ $inc: { attempts: 1 } }` adds `1` to the existing numeric value of `attempts`
options.E: `{ $pull: { subjects: "Science" } }` removes `"Science"` from the `subjects` array

answer.explanation: `$set` replaces a field's value (A), `$inc` adds to a numeric field (D), `$push` adds an element to an array, and `$pull` removes matching elements from an array (E). (Key Takeaway: `$set` assigns values, `$inc` increments numbers, `$push` appends to arrays, and `$pull` removes from arrays.)

question.stem: An engineer is deciding between `db.students.deleteOne({ age: 17 })`, `db.students.deleteMany({ age: 17 })`, and `db.students.deleteMany({})`; which statements are true (Select all that apply)?

options.A: `db.students.deleteOne({ age: 17 })` deletes all documents where `age` equals `17`
options.B: `db.students.deleteMany({ age: 17 })` deletes every document in `students` where `age` equals `17`
options.C: `db.students.deleteMany({})` drops the `students` collection and all of its indexes from `schoolDB`
options.D: `db.students.deleteMany({})` deletes all documents in `students` without dropping the collection itself
options.E: `db.students.deleteOne({ age: 17 })` deletes the `age` field from the document while keeping the document in `students`

answer.explanation: `deleteMany({ age: 17 })` removes every document where `age` equals `17` (B), and `deleteMany({})` with an empty filter deletes all documents in the collection without dropping the collection itself (D). `deleteOne({ age: 17 })` deletes the entire first matching document. (Key Takeaway: `deleteMany(filter)` removes all matching documents, and `deleteMany({})` empties the collection without dropping it.)
